Actually, the definition of Hacking is actually rather simple. It is the process of gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or systems, by way of bypassing or otherwise exploiting weaknesses in the said system's security.

As for how it works, you should visit the Deep Web and ask around, then come back here and report your findings.

Depends. A lot of what gets referred to as "hacking" in the media is actually something like ddos, which isn't hacking (ddos is just generating enough traffic to overwhelm a server).

Most common form of hacking is social engineering, which is literally just calling/emailing someone and tricking them into giving you their password. Or persuading customer support that you're someone else and forgot your password, so the customer service agent goes outside the rules to help the "customer."

Otherwise, hacking is exploiting vulnerabilities in various software to elevate your privileges within a system or to execute code you shouldn't be able to (generally with an unsanitized input somewhere). Finding the vulnerabilities often just means trying every known vulnerability until you find one the target hasn't patched.

Going further, hacking can also refer to manipulating or exploiting vulnerabilities in hardware for some purpose. For example, phreaking is a term used to describe the hacking of old telephone systems to say, make free long distance calls.
It's the same concept: you use a vulnerability that hasn't been patched yet.

It used to be that payphones could also be tricked with a matchbook. You placed a coin in and pressed it down. By jamming a matchbook in there, it would stay held down, and wouldn't require additional money for additional time. That was simple hacking.

You're right that the term "hacker" has been misappropriated from a term to describe a hobbyist who developed the first computers and software to a malicious actor. This is an unfortunate development, which reflects a world where companies frown upon the modification of systems and the use of free software.

Nowadays the term "hacking" refers to the exploitation of weaknesses in a computer network or computer system. Portrayals in the media vary in accuracy, but generally, the media tends to get purpose and tactics wrong. While movies and TV tend to show it as some sort of race to beat some sort of antivirus or encryption, real life hacking is a lot more nuanced. Hacking, in computer security, is solving a puzzle. Sometimes this puzzle has multiple solutions, sometimes it has none. The job of a computer security hacker is to get enough of the pieces to solve the puzzle and elevate access without arousing suspicion.

The important thing to know is that the puzzle is always different, and may not even involve technology. It could be something technical, like figuring out how to get into an admiration panel. But hacking could also be cold calling people and trying to get them to give you their password. It's about challenging the people, process and technology of a system.

Hacking just means that someone else has had unauthorized access to either your server or personal device. So if someone has picked up your phone and used it to go into your Facebook account both your phone and your Facebook would have been "hacked". That's the way the law, at least in UK, counts it as a crime.

Hacking is not the appropriate word for what you think of as "hacking", which is really cracking. I guess that's just semantics though.

Most of these attacks are just simple social engineering. Trickery, personal knowledge about your target, phishing, weak passwords, and the like. Another common way people are cracked is because exploits are found in software and patched by the creator(s) but the end user doesn't update their software or configure it properly to avoid security risks. It may seem simple but people may not think about updating stuff like their router's firmware. Many botnets (i.e. large amounts of computers exploited and used for nefarious purposes by the cracker) are created by exploiting weaknesses in router firmware. Some people make (and sometimes sell) software that target these common vulnerabilities, giving rise to "script kiddies" (wannabe crackers who only use cracking tools someone else invented). Only very rarely do people find a novel exploit (called a 0-day) to attack their targets. These are typically saved for a special occasion because once they're used it's eaiser to detect and start fixing it.

Ugh, I hate defining 'hack/hacker/hacking' the same way as the media.... but other people in this thread have that handled... so I'll try to just describe 'how hacking' works in as simple terms as I can...

The simplest way I can describe it is... once you know how something works, you can imagine ways it could break.

If you understand the finer details of how a given system works, you can see where weakenesses in the system exist.

The weakness is often the user, thus, why social engineering is a popular tactic to gain unauthorized access to systems.

Sometimes, its a piece of software or a software stack. If you have the understanding of how it works from the ground up, you can either break it, or make it do something its not intended to do (such as granting you access when its not supposed to).

I think you really need to go back to a time where there were two different terms - "hacking" vs "cracking". What we hear about all the time these days, particularly in the media, is malicious hacking which really relates more to what was traditionally referred to as "cracking". Perhaps you'd consider "cracking" a subset of "hacking" but alas these days everything and anything concerning technology, networking, and software is lumped in as "hacking" and the term is painted with negative connotations. Of course this has nothing to do with really answering your questions regarding how it actually works - others can attempt to explain that to you in an ELI5 format (or perhaps I'll attempt to tackle it in a different post). But just note that a kid playing with his toy remote control car who might figure out how to rewire it to go faster is essentially "hacking" - he/she is modifying it in a way that was not originally intended or anticipated by the creators; in this scenario there isn't really anything inherently malicious or harmful from this "hack".
